newsitem.title: UK: NatWest admits weak controls in option losses.
newsitem.headline: NatWest admits weak controls in option losses.

text.p: National Westminster Bank admitted Thursday that weakness in its control procedures had contributed to losses of 90 million pounds ($150 million) in options trading which were concealed for more than two years.

The Serious Fraud Office, which investigates cases of serious financial fraud, announced it was actively considering launching a criminal investigation after the bank said the losses were deliberately hidden over two years by the creation of false profits and unauthorised transfers.
"The losses ... went undiscovered because of deliberate concealment and weaknesses in the operations and internal controls in this area," the bank said in a statement.
"The independent price checking regime ... did not have sufficiently robust procedures for procuring external quotations and checking the pricing of options."
NatWest said improvements to the system, which were already being made, had helped detect the losses in February.
It also said that recommendations for improvements to the controls and risk management systems made by the investigation team were already being implemented.

The loss will show up as 77 million pounds ($128 million) in the books of the bank's investment banking unit, NatWest Markets, after taking into account provisions and the clawing back of 8 million pounds ($13.3 million) in bonuses.
The bank had already admitted that the affair had led to poor trading in the first half of this year and last week issued a profits warning affecting the whole group.
It also announced that NatWest Markets Chief Executive Martin Owen had left the firm and that Group Chief Executive Derek Wanless will run the investment bank for the time being.
NatWest said Thursday that the losses, contrary to rumours in financial circles, were confined to its interest-rate options business.

Five senior staff at NatWest Markets resigned after it was found that the losses went undiscovered due to deliberate concealment and control weakness and that trader Kyriacos Papouis, who left NatWest in December, covered up losses and created false profits over two years.

The report into the losses, first discovered in February, by law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants Coopers & Lybrand, said the losses -- in German mark and pound sterling interest rate options -- had been due to poor trading and adverse market conditions.
The losses were then covered up by deliberate mis-pricing and over-valuing of options contracts.
NatWest said, however, that there was no evidence of client loss and no personal gain "as a result of collusion with third parties."
But NatWest said the full report was not being published for legal and commercial reasons, although it had been sent to the Bank of England and the Securities and Futures Authority.
The Serious Fraud Office had also been fully briefed, it said.
